comparison: Both evaluate the identification of transitional EMT cells with elevated RiBi (C27-C32). OpenEval finds strong support through convergence of multiple measurements. Peer reviewers explicitly affirmed this as a core discovery, describing it as 'convincing and solid' with 'state of the art technology.' Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with high confidence.

Both address scRNA-seq evidence for RiBi elevation during EMT transitions (C33-C40). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive analytical approaches and statistical significance. Peer reviewers accepted this as part of the core finding that RiBi is activated during transitional states. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED, though peer review groups this with C27-C32 as a unified discovery.

Perfect claim overlap (C41-C45) on RiBi upregulation during MET. OpenEval notes modest sample size (n=3 mice) but finds evidence consistent and SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accepted this as complementary evidence for bidirectional RiBi role in transitions, treating it as part of the overall conclusion. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Perfect claim overlap (C46-C53) on signaling pathways linking to RiBi activity. OpenEval finds convergence of multiple assays strengthens the result (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this molecular characterization as part of their assessment that the study used 'state of the art technology' with 'convincing' conclusions. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address pharmacological RiBi inhibition blocking EMT/MET (C56-C59). OpenEval notes two independent inhibitors strengthen conclusions despite modest sample sizes (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers accepted the blocking effect but requested clarification about specificity versus general growth inhibition, which was apparently addressed in revisions. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED, though peer review initially raised mechanistic questions.

Both evaluate genetic validation via ribosomal protein knockdown (C61-C62). OpenEval notes consistent phenotypes but acknowledges reliance on cited work for mechanism and potential off-target effects (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers grouped this with pharmacological inhibition data and accepted it after revisions addressed concerns about transition-specific versus general effects. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Perfect claim overlap (C63-C66) on drug synergy. OpenEval finds quantitative synergy scores and multiple drugs strengthen conclusions but notes minimal replication (n=2 wells, SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers explicitly affirmed synergistic effects as a key finding, though editor noted additional mechanistic support would strengthen the study. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with minor reservations about mechanistic specificity.

Perfect claim overlap (C67-C72) on in vivo validation of combination therapy. OpenEval finds comprehensive evidence with appropriate experimental design and adequate statistics (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers affirmed impaired metastasis and described the study as having 'high clinical relevance' with 'quite solid' evidence. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with high confidence.

Perfect claim overlap (C73-C74) on human cell line validation. OpenEval finds this strengthens generalizability though only one human line was tested (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers did not specifically critique this but implicitly accepted it as part of their assessment of 'high clinical relevance.' Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address patient sample analysis (C75-C76). OpenEval finds two samples insufficient for strong conclusions and describes the analysis as exploratory (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers did not challenge the human relevance data and accepted it as supporting evidence for clinical relevance. OpenEval is more critical (UNCERTAIN) while peer review implicitly accepts it (SUPPORTED) as secondary evidence.

Both evaluate large patient cohort analysis (C77). OpenEval notes large sample sizes but criticizes arbitrary cutoffs, lack of causation, and missing confounding factor analysis (SUPPORTED but with caveats). Peer reviewers grouped this with C75-C76 and accepted it as supporting translational relevance without specific critique. Both are SUPPORTED but OpenEval is more critical of methodological details.

Both address the main therapeutic conclusion (C11). OpenEval finds this is an inference beyond the data requiring clinical validation (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers found the therapeutic potential 'valuable' and of 'high clinical relevance' but noted additional mechanistic support would strengthen claims about EMT/MET specificity (UNCERTAIN). Both express reservations about mechanistic certainty despite accepting therapeutic promise.

Minimal overlap (C86 only). OpenEval evaluates summary claims C5-C7, C83-C86 as supported by detailed results but notes 'essential' may be overstated (SUPPORTED). Peer review R9 addresses broader therapeutic implications C8-C11, C86 with uncertainty about mechanistic specificity. Different focus areas with limited direct comparison.
